name: Original Plum Torte
headnote: Marian Burros's plum torte ran in The Times every September from 1983 to 1989, when editors tried to retire it and were met with a flood of protest letters from readers who treated its yearly appearance as the marker of summer turning to fall. The paper relented and now keeps it permanently available. The original 1983 version used 1 cup of sugar; the 1989 revision cut that to three-quarters of a cup, and both amounts are offered.
comment_digest: The single most-voted thread (4,607 votes, answered at 4,106) is a measuring question that changes the outcome: "sifted flour" means sift first then measure, while "flour, sifted" means measure then sift, so the cup here should be measured after sifting. Many bakers report the torte works with other fruit - raspberries and blackberries in place of plums (1,955 votes), with a third of the flour swapped for cornmeal. A 1,397-vote note prefers slicing the plums and fanning them over the batter rather than pressing in halves: prettier and more evenly distributed, and suggests lemon zest and sliced almonds. Several comments are affectionate anecdotes rather than technique.

name: Panettone
headnote: A classic panettone from Italian pastry chef Andrea Tortora, presented as a project demanding careful timing and patience rather than difficulty of technique. The site frames it as the definitive symbol of an Italian Christmas, aromatic and complex, and notes that the loaves must be hung upside down to cool on knitting needles or thin wooden dowels pushed through the base.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: non-NYT site (Great Italian Chefs); no comments section and no rating; batch url had an NYT share parameter appended but the page is greatitalianchefs.com

name: Simple Steak Au Poivre
headnote: NYT Cooking presents steak au poivre as far less daunting than its reputation: a sauteed steak finished with a fast pan sauce. This version leans on both black peppercorns and Sichuan pepper, which keeps it bright rather than aggressively hot or boozy. Scallion mashed potatoes are suggested alongside.
comment_digest: The two highest-voted notes are both about the pan. One (180 votes) warns to sear in light-coloured stainless steel rather than a dark pan so you can watch the fond: burn it and the sauce is ruined. A follow-up (55 votes) cautions against preheating cast iron on the highest burner setting and suggests preheating the pan in a 350F oven instead to avoid setting off smoke alarms. A 268-vote comment describes keeping jars of mixed peppercorns steeped in brandy for a couple of months as a standing substitution. Others adjust the sauce toward heavy cream with more butter and only a little beef broth, and several with thick 8 oz filets sear both sides then finish in the oven, since the stovetop-only timing leaves them raw in the centre.

name: Sourdough No-Knead Bread
headnote: Sam Sifton's adaptation of Jim Lahey's no-knead loaf for people who have a live sourdough starter and want something to do with it. Commercial yeast is replaced by just under three-quarters of a cup of well-fed starter, the dough gets a very long rise, and it bakes covered in a preheated enameled cast-iron pot.
comment_digest: The top note (764 votes) is a handling fix: line the rising vessel with parchment and lift the dough into the hot pot by the paper, which ends the mess of flour-dusted towels. The single biggest point of confusion (613 votes) is what "fed" starter means in practice; the best-voted answers say to build the starter up so it is at peak activity, and to use the float test - a spoonful dropped in water should float before you mix (165 votes). A 320-vote comment questions why this bakes at 550F when standard no-knead bakes at 450F; an experienced baker (237 votes) preheats a cast-iron Dutch oven to 500F and drops to 450F once the loaf goes in. Rating is 4 stars, lower than most, consistent with the timing ambiguity.

name: Sourdough Pancake or Waffle Batter
headnote: A use for the starter discard that would otherwise go in the bin when you feed a sourdough culture. The discard becomes the base of a batter that ferments overnight and is cooked as pancakes or waffles the next morning, giving a lot of tangy flavour for very little active work. Part of Sam Sifton's sourdough coverage.
comment_digest: The most-voted thread is a running argument about weight versus volume that matters directly for gram conversion. One note (369 votes) points out that a cup of a liquid and a cup of a solid do not weigh the same - a cup of water is 8 oz or about 230 grams, and flour, being less dense, weighs appreciably less - so a single gram figure cannot be applied to every cup in a recipe. A 281-vote comment thanks the Times for printing grams at all and argues cups and teaspoons are the unreliable measure; a 301-vote reply pushes back that scales vary too. On technique, plain yogurt substitutes cleanly for buttermilk (232 votes), and a 135-vote note replaces all or part of the all-purpose flour with wholewheat, oat or other flours without trouble.
flags: top comments are a volume-vs-grams debate rather than recipe technique

name: Spiced Chickpea Stew with Coconut and Turmeric
headnote: Alison Roman's stew - the one that went viral as "the stew" - crisps spiced chickpeas in olive oil and then simmers them in garlicky coconut milk, adding stock, sturdy leafy greens and a finishing handful of mint. The headnote nods to South Indian and Caribbean stews. It warns explicitly against low-fat coconut milk, drinking coconut milk and cream of coconut, none of which will work.
comment_digest: The top note (1,905 votes) lists the changes people find make it better: a jalapeno with the onion, garlic and ginger, double the onion, and more seasoning throughout. A 640-vote comment and a 949-vote rebuttal disagree over the two cans of coconut milk - some cut to one, others use both and find it fine - and several cooks say the dish needs added acid, usually lemon or lime juice at the end, which the recipe omits. A 1,013-vote note gives a homemade coconut milk formula: blend 1 3/4 cups unsweetened shredded coconut with 2 1/3 cups warm water. A 590-vote comment argues against all the tinkering and says to follow it as written. Practical aside at 1,599 votes: keep ginger in the freezer and grate it frozen.

name: Spinach Lasagna with Fennel Sausage
headnote: A from-scratch holiday lasagna, pasta included, that the headnote openly calls a time-consuming project worth doing - ideally with a helper or spread across two days. Store-bought fresh or dried noodles and your own tomato sauce are sanctioned shortcuts. The result is described as delicate and rich enough that small portions are right.
comment_digest: Comment volume is low, so vote counts are small. The most-voted note (14) says the fresh pasta sheets do not need pre-cooking - they cook through in the sauce - though a 10-vote comment from someone who has made it two Christmases running recommends cooking them and, more usefully, says the bechamel needs only 4 cups of milk rather than 5, as 5 is too loose. An 8-vote note suggests crushed fennel seeds added to the filling to echo the sausage, plus sauteed mushrooms or carrots. Another swaps broccoli rabe into the filling, blanching chopped stems first and the leaves a minute later. Several cooks confirm the time commitment is real.
flags: only 39 comments, so vote counts are in single/low double digits

name: Strawberry Eton Mess
headnote: The traditional British assembly of fresh fruit, whipped cream and crushed meringue, pitched here as a hot-weather dessert with almost no cooking. Store-bought meringue cookies are explicitly fine, which reduces it to a mixing job. Lime zest and juice are added for a sweet-tart edge, with lemon offered as an alternative.
comment_digest: The highest-voted comments (229 and 81 votes) are a pointed objection to other readers who substitute cookies or cake for the meringue: without meringue it is a trifle, not an Eton mess, and they urge anyone wanting that to use a different recipe. A 135-vote note confirms the classic form is meringue, whipped cream and strawberries. On execution, a 122-vote comment halved the recipe for two but accidentally used the full tablespoon of lime juice and found the extra acid a marked improvement, implying the stated amount is conservative. Fruit swaps that work: raspberries, peaches, and blueberries heated until they pop for the syrup with more raw berries folded in. Trader Joe's is named as a source for meringue cookies.

name: Summer Pasta with Zucchini, Ricotta and Basil
headnote: A deliberately plain summer pasta built on garden or market zucchini, fresh ricotta and basil. The headnote's main instruction is about shopping rather than technique: seek out good artisanal ricotta, because with this few components the quality of each one shows.
comment_digest: The top note (1,349 votes) changes the method: combine the ricotta, red pepper flakes and lemon zest in a large bowl with enough pasta water to loosen them into a sauce before the pasta goes in, rather than adding them to the pan. A 1,144-vote comment says to cook the garlic together with the onions - it will not burn since everything is sweating - and treats the dish as a template open to variation. Two independent notes (643 and 456 votes) push for more browning and more seasoning: let some onion and zucchini go past soft to genuinely caramelized, do not skimp on the red pepper flakes, and double the lemon zest. A 404-vote comment complains the written steps are fussier than the dish warrants and needs constant re-reading.

name: Summer Shrimp Scampi with Tomatoes and Corn
headnote: A one-skillet scampi that swaps the usual pasta context for peak-summer corn and tomatoes. A very hot pan is the point: the tomatoes blister and the corn caramelizes before everything gets coated in garlic-lemon butter. It is meant to stand alone as a meal, with pasta or bread optional.
comment_digest: The highest-voted practical note (271 votes) restructures the sequence to cut prep fuss: start the tomatoes in olive oil, push them aside once blistered, add the corn to the cleared space, and carry on from there in the one pan. Protein swaps are well attested - scallops sauteed in butter instead of olive oil, with only another 2 tablespoons of butter at the end (138 votes), and lobster meat (100 votes) - all reported as working. A 158-vote comment cut the butter back for a lighter weeknight version and was happy with it, while conceding the full amount would taste better. A 114-vote variant skips cooking the vegetables entirely: marinate raw corn and tomatoes in a lemon, garlic and basil vinaigrette and fold in seared shrimp.

name: Swiss Chard Ravioli
headnote: Giuliano Hazan's ravioli, filled with Swiss chard, ricotta and prosciutto in a tender handmade pasta. The Washington Post drew it from his online Homemade Italian Pasta class and tested it with a plain sage-butter sauce, noting that a tomato sauce also works if used sparingly. They close with Hazan quoting his mother Marcella on keeping the sauce subordinate to the pasta.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: washingtonpost.com - headnote present, no comments or rating on the page; the url redirected to the same recipe without the trailing id

name: Takeout-Style Sesame Noodles
headnote: Sam Sifton's version of the cold peanut-butter-based sesame noodles that became a Chinese-American standard in 1970s New York. The headnote credits the dish to Shorty Tang, who came from Sichuan via Taipei and opened Hwa Yuan in Chinatown in 1967; his family still serves it and has never released the recipe, so this is the Times' own reconstruction.
comment_digest: The step people get wrong is the noodle quantity (1,121 votes): the pound called for is fresh or frozen noodles, not dried, so anyone reaching for a dried pound is badly overshooting the sauce. The most-voted note overall (2,086) says thick supermarket noodles give a close approximation when proper Chinese noodles are unavailable. A 1,541-vote comment from someone who has made it many times for crowds multiplies the sauce with a stick blender and uses only a minimal amount of the hottest element. An 868-vote note treats it as a picnic dish with condiments served alongside - shredded duck or chicken, tofu, cucumber, sweet pepper, scallion, jicama. For gram conversion: a 674-vote comment makes sesame paste from scratch with 200g toasted sesame seeds blended with 5-6 tablespoons olive oil.
flags: gram datapoint: homemade sesame paste = 200 g toasted sesame seeds + 5-6 tbsp olive oil (674 votes)

name: Tartine’s Country Bread
headnote: Chad Robertson's cult loaf from Tartine Bakery in San Francisco, adapted by the Times for a home kitchen: a tangy open crumb inside a blistered dark crust, raised entirely on a starter you build yourself. Allow roughly two weeks from nothing, or two days if your starter is already active. The headnote is candid that the outcome is not fully controllable - starter vigour, kitchen humidity, rise temperature and your own timing all shift the result.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (599) is a source for a free starter by mail from the Oregon Trail Sourdough Preservation Society, sidestepping the two-week build. The recurring complaint (318 votes) is how much starter the method discards - most of it during the build, then all but a tablespoon for the bake - and a 235-vote comment says step 3's wording is what confuses people: the night before baking you keep only 1 tablespoon of mature starter and build the leaven from that. A 166-vote comment reports the loaves come out just as well without the three-plus hours of turn-and-fold, which is the most substantive disagreement with the method. A 255-vote reader put the whole schedule into a spreadsheet with date/time formulas to track the stages.

name: The Silver Palate’s Chicken Marbella
headnote: Christine Muhlke's framing of the Sheila Lukins and Julee Rosso dish from "The Silver Palate Cookbook" (1982), which reached the Times in a 2007 piece marking the book's 25th anniversary. The chicken marinates with prunes, olives, capers and oregano - a sweet-briny pairing that read as daring in the eighties and now reads as a standard.
comment_digest: The most useful correction (1,328 votes) is a scaling error: this NYT version halves the original cookbook's ingredients except for the wine and the brown sugar, which stayed at full quantity - so the sugar on top is roughly double what it should be. A former Silver Palate kitchen cook confirms it (861 votes), saying the brown sugar was only ever a light dusting, and adds a technique note: crisp the skin a little before dusting. Two well-voted substitutions: dried apricots for the prunes with much less sugar, served with couscous and roast butternut (1,115 votes), and boneless thighs instead of bone-in pieces, which guests find easier and which shortens the roasting time (997 votes). The single highest-voted comment (2,447) is a request for a site feature, not recipe content.
flags: top-voted comment by votes is a site feature request, not recipe content; real technique lead is the brown-sugar scaling error

name: Thomas Keller’s Butternut Squash Soup with Brown Butter
headnote: An adaptation of the butternut squash soup in Thomas Keller's "Bouchon," presented frankly as a four-hour undertaking that includes making your own vegetable stock. The payoff is a soup of unusual depth, finished by swirling in sizzling brown butter just before serving.
comment_digest: The step that trips people up is the squash prep (541 votes): the recipe has you cut the neck off and roast only the bulb, then work with the raw neck in the next step, which reads as contradictory until you notice it. Two well-voted comments propose simplifying it - poke and roast the squash whole (670 votes), or split it lengthwise and roast both halves for more caramelization (400 votes), with the 400-vote commenter noting 25 years of making it this way despite the recipe's instruction. A 522-vote tip: do not throw away the thick paste left in the strainer; chill it and mix with Parmesan as ravioli filling. A 202-vote note keeps a freezer bag of vegetable scraps going so the stock step is not a separate shopping trip.

name: Toasted Almond Biscotti
comment_digest: With only nine comments the votes are tiny, but they converge on one clear fault: the first bake is too short. Multiple cooks (5 votes, 2 votes and an unvoted note) found raw dough in the centre when they went to slice the log at the stated 15 minutes; one cites Jacques Pepin's biscotti as baking 25 minutes at 350F for the first bake and 30 to 40 for the second, and another added 10 minutes to the sliced cookies and found the flavour improved as well. A 4-vote comment credits the recipe with two genuine advantages over others: the almond-toasting method, and a dough that slices without crumbling, possibly because the oven temperature is lower. One cook doubled it using 1 1/2 cups almond flour plus 1 cup self-rising flour for a more tender result. A further objection is that the recipe never specifies which flour to use.
flags: no headnote on the page - only a 'Featured in' line; comment votes are single digits

name: Tuna-Salad Sandwich, Julia Child Style
headnote: Dorie Greenspan's account of what Julia Child ate for a working lunch when she was home between trips. Per her longtime assistant Stephanie Hersh, only two things were fixed - oil-packed tuna and Hellmann's mayonnaise - and everything else was negotiable. The suggested build adds capers, cornichons, chopped onion, lemon juice and herbs, served open-face on an English muffin or on white bread.
comment_digest: This thread is dominated by reminiscence rather than technique, so the vote counts reward anecdote: the top comment (503 votes) is a joke about Duke's mayonnaise being better than Hellmann's, and the next several (420, 342, 264, 218 votes) are personal stories about Julia Child and about tuna sandwiches generally, with no cooking content. The one substantive technique note (109 votes) recommends peeling the celery before chopping it - it removes the stringy outer layer and markedly improves the texture, which the commenter concedes sounds like French fussiness but considers worth doing. Little disagreement with the recipe itself appears; the 4-star rating seems to reflect that it is barely a recipe.
flags: comments are mostly anecdote; only one real technique point (peel the celery)

name: Turmeric Rice--Franey
comment_digest: Only two comments. The more useful one (3 votes) warns that the site carries two different Pierre Franey turmeric rice recipes and argues this one is the better side dish, using considerably less turmeric and water rather than stock - worth knowing if a differently-proportioned version turns up elsewhere in the collection. The other reports it works fine with jasmine rice in place of the specified rice, came together easily, and pairs well with the site's roasted shrimp cocktail with aioli.
flags: no headnote, only a 'Featured in: 60-Minute Gourmet' line; byline confirmed as Pierre Franey, matching the batch name; page title is 'Turmeric Rice' without the Franey suffix; only 2 comments; a second distinct Franey turmeric rice exists on the site

name: Umbrian-Style Chicken Alla Cacciatora
headnote: Julia Moskin's write-up of the central-Italian version of hunter's chicken, which predates the arrival of tomatoes and therefore has none. Lemon, vinegar, olives and rosemary carry the dish instead of the southern tomato sauce Americans expect. She suggests serving it over mashed potatoes or polenta with steamed greens dressed in fruity olive oil.
comment_digest: The whole thread turns on one disputed step. A 202-vote comment questions step 2, which returns the seared chicken to the pan with raw onions rather than waiting for them to soften, and a 33-vote reply argues that cooking the onions to caramelized would overcook the chicken given the later simmer. The recipe's own author answers (106 votes) and settles it: adding the raw onions to the chicken is intentional, the onions will collapse into the wine anyway, and the perceived timing problem comes from searing the chicken in batches, which takes longer than people expect. She adds two things the recipe does not say - never pit the olives, since the pits flavour the braise, and organic chicken will take a long simmer without drying out. A 42-vote commenter who cooked it with the author in Assisi says change nothing. Roasting it in the oven also works (33 votes).

name: Wagshal’s Boeuf Bourguignon
headnote: The Washington Post's version of the boeuf bourguignon sold at Wagshal's, the long-running market in the District's Spring Valley neighbourhood, where it is among the best-selling prepared dishes. The Post's one serving note is to put garlic-rubbed toast alongside so none of the sauce is wasted.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: batch url was only the washingtonpost.com homepage; located the actual recipe at /recipes/wagshals-boeuf-bourguignon/ and recorded that url. No comments or rating on WaPo recipe pages

name: Whole Roasted New York Strip Loin
headnote: An argument for roasting a whole strip loin - the cut normally sliced into New York or Kansas City strip steaks - as a holiday centrepiece, positioned as cheaper than tenderloin or standing rib while still impressive. Served with roasted potatoes and parsnips and horseradish sauce.
comment_digest: The comments largely argue against the recipe's method, which is why the rating sits at 4. The top note (135 votes) advocates the reverse sear: start the room-temperature roast at 180-200F with a probe in it, cook until it reaches target, then blast it to finish. A 42-vote comment says roasting an expensive cut at a flat 400F produces a mediocre result and urges searing each side first. A 99-vote reply defends the recipe's logic on Maillard grounds, arguing the browning flavours need sustained high heat that low-and-slow alone will not give. Useful doneness reference from a 28-vote professional chef: bleu is 115-120F, rare (saignant) 125-130F, medium rare above that. A cook who followed it exactly on a 10 lb prime loin pulled at 127F and rested under foil with good results.
flags: top comments dispute the recipe's roasting method rather than endorse it

name: Whole-Wheat Buttermilk Pancakes
headnote: A 100 percent whole-wheat pancake that sets out to avoid the density that reputation attaches to them. The trick is resting the batter for the five minutes the pan takes to heat, which lets the bran and germ hydrate and soften so the pancakes stay tender while keeping the nutty whole-wheat flavour.
comment_digest: The most valuable thread for anyone working in weights is a flour discrepancy. Commenters (44 and 30 votes) reported that 270 grams of whole-wheat flour is well over the 1 1/2 cups the recipe then stated, and that measuring by volume gave a soupy batter - one habitual weigher confirmed it after measuring by cup for once. NYT has since corrected the listing, which now reads 2 1/2 cups/270 grams, so anyone working from an older copy should use the gram figure. Several cooks who followed it as written, including the rest, call the pancakes light and fluffy and among the best whole-wheat pancakes they have had (55 and 24 votes). A 59-vote note calculates roughly 160 calories per pancake before oil or toppings.
flags: gram datapoint: whole-wheat flour 2 1/2 cups = 270 g (recipe was corrected after comments flagged 1 1/2 cups as wrong; also buttermilk 2 cups = 480 ml per the ingredient list)

name: Zucchini Gratin
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: foodnetwork.com - Ina Garten, from 'Barefoot in Paris'. No headnote text on the page, only recipe metadata. Rated 4.5 of 5 from 449 reviews but the review bodies do not render in the DOM, so no comment content could be extracted

name: Chinese Smashed Cucumbers With Sesame Oil And Garlic
headnote: Julia Moskin on pai huang gua, the smashed cucumber salad eaten across China as a counter to hot weather and hot food, sometimes with dried chiles and Sichuan peppercorns. Smashing is the point: it cracks the skin, loosens the seeds and breaks the flesh into rough pieces that hold dressing. Salting and chilling afterwards draws out water and delivers the cold, crunchy texture the dish depends on.
comment_digest: Two well-voted comments argue the recipe is missing an authentic component. A reader who ate this regularly in Sichuan (413 votes) says to toast Sichuan peppercorns until fragrant, crush them and add them to the dressing; a 319-vote comment repeats the Sichuan pepper point and additionally swaps the rice wine vinegar for Chinkiang-style aged dark vinegar, whose sorghum base suits the dish better. On method, a 624-vote note offers a shortcut: scoop the seeds first, smash lightly, then spread the pieces on a plate to dry rather than salting and draining. A 303-vote comment reassures cooks anxious about smashing technique that precision does not matter much. The highest-voted note overall (1,621) is a joke about using the drained cucumber water for a gin martini.

name: Cucumber Salad With Roasted Peanuts and Chile
headnote: Sue Li's layered cucumber salad, built from four contrasting elements: salted cucumbers, a peanut sauce, a chopped peanut and cilantro topping, and chile oil. The headnote explains why each step exists - salting suppresses the cucumber's faint bitterness and concentrates flavour, the peanut sauce supplies richness against the cold cucumber, and the dry topping is scattered in layers rather than all at once so the flavour is distributed. The sauce is worth making in quantity to keep in the fridge.
comment_digest: The most consequential item is an editor's reply (290 votes) acknowledging a reader was right that the cutting instruction was unclear: the recipe has since been revised to say cut the cucumbers lengthwise into thin spears first, then crosswise - so an older printed copy will have the vaguer wording. An 86-vote note from the same thread says peeled regular cucumbers work as well as English ones, and that larger cucumbers should be halved and seeded given that the dish is about texture. A 184-vote comment learned a Thai version that uses fish sauce in place of soy sauce and cuts the cucumbers differently. An 84-vote cook found the dressing too salty and plans to leave out the kosher salt entirely next time, which is worth weighing against the salting step. The 415-vote note is sarcasm about a commenter who ignored the recipe and then blamed it.
